newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn to sell rest of Lufthansa in autumn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn to sell rest of Lufthansa in autumn.

text.p: The German government on Thursday detailed the five-billion-mark privatisation of Bonn's remaining stake in the airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG aimed at keeping a majority stake in German hands.

A joint statement from the transport and finance ministries, along with the government development agency Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau (KfW), said the KfW will sell the remaining 36 percent stake in the autumn.
The issue volume will be five billion marks ($2.7 billion), based on current share valuations, the statement said.
The KfW, which has acted as temporary trustee for the shares since December 1996, said it would also sell a 1.77 percent stake in the airline, which it has held for some time, in the flotation.
Dresdner Kleinwort Benson and SBC Warburg are to act as global coordinators of the Lufthansa sale, Germany's second-biggest initial public offering (IPO) to date, the statement said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell will act as senior co-lead manager, with DG Bank and Merrill Lynch as co-lead managers.
The government said the make-up of the issuing consortium should ensure that at least 50 percent of the shares would remain in German hands.

This would be achieved by making Germany the main focus of the share placement. Ensuring that a majority stake remains in German hands has been one of the stumbling blocks in completing the flotation.
The European Commission has wanted assurances from Bonn that ownership of Lufthansa would remain with Germans.
International air law requires flag carriers to show that national shareholders hold majority stakes if they are to retain their rights.

Many of around 200 bilateral air traffic agreements between Germany and other countries stipulate that Lufthansa must remain in the hands of German investors, a condition which is hard to keep to if the shares are freely floated.

"With special consideration for German investors, this (flotation) should strengthen Germany as a financial centre and help develop an equity culture in Germany following the positive experiences of the Deutsche Telekom IPO," the government said.
Bonn received 2.1 billion marks for the 35.68 percent stake when it parked it with KfW last year. This was budgeted for in 1996.
As the issue volume is valued at five billion marks, the 2.9 billion marks difference from the sale to the private sector will accrue to Bonn's coffers and be budgeted in 1997.

The procedure of parking the shares with KfW before selling on to the private sector is not unusual in Germany, and happened previously when the government sold its stake in the utility giant Viag AG.

Lufthansa was partially privatised in 1994. The German government has been keen to whip its finances into shape in advance of European currency union, due to start in 1999, but with many of the budgetary criteria for membership needing to be met in 1997.
